posts.title: A whole research paper in Quarto
posts.source_date_evidence: Public LinkedIn SocialMediaPosting metadata retrieved 9 November 2026
posts.original_post_text:
Did you know that you can go from data preparation to a PDF manuscript of a paper with a single click?

I took the GitHub repository for the May 2024 version of "Contagion Effects of the Silicon Valley Bank Run" (graciously provided by the authors Paul Goldsmith-Pinkham, Dong Beom Choi and Tanju Yorulmazer) and used it as a "demo" of the idea putting a whole paper in Quarto.

Building on Pandoc, LaTex, knitr, and more, Quarto takes care of details like numbering sections, producing citations and a reference list, and more.

The resulting PDF is here: https://lnkd.in/exw77kEb

The source code is here: https://lnkd.in/eBeF8ZRF

posts.title: ChatGPT as a copy editor, with Git
posts.source_date_evidence: Public LinkedIn SocialMediaPosting metadata retrieved 9 November 2026
posts.original_post_text:
ChatGPT is a pretty awesome copy editor (I guess other AIs are too). It picks up not only typos, but even issues in code and inconsistencies in data-handling. At times it is too willing to say "here is revised text …", but then you tell it that you want notes and feedback, not edited text.

It also works very nicely with Git. Git is such a great tool for complex writing projects (e.g., a book or paper with a lot of code) and is nicely integrated into RStudio. Though there is a bit of a learning curve, especially for "off label" use cases. 

(The screenshot below shows things mostly caught by ChatGPT ... it also found two [fortunately very minor] errors in my code.)

posts.title: Severance and academic incentives
posts.source_date_evidence: Public LinkedIn SocialMediaPosting metadata retrieved 9 November 2026
posts.original_post_text:
I see interesting connections between the work of the severed employees of the "macrodata refinement department" in Severance (Apple TV+) and academic research.

I see parallels between how both the severed employees of MDR and many academics attach meaning to what they do.

Mark suggests that the work is "mysterious and important" but one can't tell if he believes this, or is just fulfilling his role as a leader. (In the first season, the MDR employees have no idea what their work is about.)

Irving definitely seems to want to believe that "everything we do here is important", though Helly asks a good question: "It’s important because it actually is? Or because you’re saying it is?"

Dylan is all about the incentives, including erasers and finger traps for productive employees: "I'm smart. That's why I have three times as many finger traps as you guys." Replace finger traps with "top-tier publications" and many academics probably know the type.
